words.definition: a university student studying for a first degree
words.example: As an {undergraduate}, she studied chemistry at Leeds.

words.definition: a long piece of writing done as part of a degree
words.example: For her degree, she spent a year researching and writing a long {dissertation} on Scottish castles.

words.definition: a class in which a small group discusses a topic with a teacher
words.example: Only twelve students attend each {seminar}, so everyone has to speak.

words.definition: a group of related departments in a university
words.example: She teaches in the {faculty} of law.

words.definition: the land and buildings of a university
words.example: Many universities have halls where first-year students can live on {campus}.

words.definition: to complete a university degree
words.example: He hopes to {graduate} with a first in physics.

words.definition: a year off between school and university
words.example: Before starting university, she took a {gap year} to work on a farm in New Zealand.

words.definition: a booklet that describes a university and its courses
words.example: Read the {prospectus} carefully before you choose a course.

words.definition: studying for a second, higher degree
words.example: Having finished her first degree, she is now studying for a {postgraduate} degree in teaching.

words.definition: to explain something by giving examples or pictures
words.example: The teacher used a simple drawing to {illustrate} how the heart pumps blood.

words.definition: to combine ideas from different sources into one whole
words.example: A good essay should {synthesise} ideas from several sources into one clear argument.

words.definition: to judge how good or useful something is
words.example: We must {evaluate} each solution carefully before choosing one.

words.definition: to come from something, or get something from it
words.example: Many English words {derive} from Latin.

words.definition: to form or make up something
words.example: Women now {constitute} over half of the university's students.

words.definition: to make something weaker, often slowly
words.example: Constant criticism can {undermine} a child's confidence.

words.definition: to make something easier or possible
words.example: The new lift will {facilitate} access for wheelchair users.

words.definition: to speak in public in support of an idea
words.example: Many doctors {advocate} a tax on sugary drinks.

words.definition: to give something to someone for a particular purpose
words.example: The school will {allocate} each student a locker from those it already owns.

words.definition: to say that something is caused by something else
words.example: Experts {attribute} the rise in obesity to poor diet.

words.definition: including everything or almost everything
words.example: The guide gives a {comprehensive} list of the island's beaches, with every single one included.

words.definition: large in size, amount or importance
words.example: She inherited a {substantial} sum, over a million pounds, from her aunt.

words.definition: existing as a natural part of something
words.example: Danger is part of climbing itself; every climb carries an {inherent} risk.

words.definition: seeming likely to be true
words.example: It seems {plausible} that the fire started in the kitchen, though nobody can be certain.

words.definition: having more than one possible meaning
words.example: The sentence 'I saw her duck' is {ambiguous} because it has two possible meanings.

words.definition: possible to do
words.example: Is it {feasible} to finish the whole project by Friday?

words.definition: chosen by chance or on a whim, not for a reason
words.example: The referee's decision seemed {arbitrary}, with no clear reason behind it.

words.definition: stated clearly and fully
words.example: The instructions were {explicit}: no phones in the exam room.

words.definition: very deep or serious
words.example: The novel raises {profound} questions about life and death.

words.definition: very small in amount or importance
words.example: There was only a {marginal} difference between the two results.

words.definition: language used to persuade, sometimes without much real meaning
words.example: The politician's speech was full of empty {rhetoric}.

words.definition: to admit, often unwillingly, that something is true
words.example: I hate to admit it, but I {concede} that your plan is cheaper than mine.

words.definition: to prove that a statement is wrong
words.example: She used official figures to {refute} his claim, proving beyond doubt that it was false.

words.definition: a statement made firmly, as if it were certainly true
words.example: He insisted that crime had doubled, an {assertion} he could not support with evidence.

words.definition: an idea that an argument is based on
words.example: Every argument starts from a {premise}, an idea accepted as true, and ends with a conclusion.

words.definition: able to express ideas clearly in words
words.example: Although she is only twelve, she is {articulate} and explains her ideas clearly.

words.definition: to move away from the main subject when speaking or writing
words.example: Sorry, I tend to {digress}; let's get back to the main point.

words.definition: good at making people agree or believe something
words.example: She wrote a {persuasive} letter that changed the council's mind.

words.definition: a short, interesting story about a real event
words.example: He began his speech with a funny {anecdote} about his dog.

words.definition: an answer that shows an argument is wrong
words.example: In the debate, she answered her opponent with a powerful {rebuttal} that proved him wrong.

words.definition: the power of a country to rule itself
words.example: After centuries of foreign rule, the island finally won full {sovereignty} and could govern itself.

words.definition: a vote by all the people of a country on one question
words.example: The country held a {referendum} on leaving the union.

words.definition: the basic laws and principles of a country
words.example: In many countries, a written {constitution} sets out citizens' basic rights.

words.definition: a government made of two or more political parties
words.example: The two parties formed a {coalition} after the election.

words.definition: a system with too many rules, forms and officials
words.example: Opening a café involves a lot of {bureaucracy}.

words.definition: responsible for your actions and having to explain them
words.example: Politicians must be held {accountable} for their decisions.

words.definition: dishonest behaviour by people in power, for money or favours
words.example: The mayor was arrested for {corruption}.

words.definition: demanding that everyone obeys those in power
words.example: Under the {authoritarian} regime, critical newspapers were closed.

words.definition: to try to persuade politicians to support something
words.example: Farmers met MPs in Parliament to {lobby} them for lower fuel prices.

words.definition: the authority that voters give to a government
words.example: The new president has a clear {mandate} for change.

words.definition: money a government gives to make something cheaper
words.example: Farmers receive a {subsidy} for growing certain crops.

words.definition: strict cuts in government spending
words.example: Years of {austerity}, with deep cuts in public spending, meant fewer libraries and youth clubs.

words.definition: a tax on goods coming into a country
words.example: A new {tariff} made foreign cars more expensive.

words.definition: connected with government money and taxes
words.example: The government announced new {fiscal} rules on borrowing.

words.definition: a product that can be bought and sold, such as oil or wheat
words.example: Oil is the most valuable {commodity} in the region.

words.definition: the amount by which spending is greater than income
words.example: The country has a huge budget {deficit}.

words.definition: a system in which businesses are privately owned for profit
words.example: Under {capitalism}, prices are mostly set by the market.

words.definition: all the jobs available and the people available to do them
words.example: Young people are finding it hard to enter the {labour market}.

words.definition: a large company that operates in many countries
words.example: The {multinational} has factories in twenty countries.

words.definition: the state of being successful and having plenty of money
words.example: Trade brought great {prosperity} to the port city.

words.definition: to make something bad less serious
words.example: Planting trees can {mitigate} the effects of flooding.

words.definition: adding no extra carbon dioxide to the air overall
words.example: By planting trees to balance its emissions, the company aims to be {carbon neutral} by 2030.

words.definition: the reduction of something until little of it is left
words.example: The {depletion} of fish stocks worries scientists.

words.definition: impossible to change back
words.example: Once a species dies out, the loss is {irreversible}: it can never be brought back.

words.definition: the process of something becoming worse in quality
words.example: Air pollution has caused the slow {degradation} of the cathedral's stone carvings.

words.definition: rain, snow or hail
words.example: The forecast shows heavy {precipitation} in the north tonight.

words.definition: connected with living things and their environment
words.example: Bees play a vital {ecological} role, keeping plants and their environment healthy.

words.definition: a person who works to protect nature
words.example: A {conservationist} has spent years protecting the island's turtles.

words.definition: letting land go back to its natural state
words.example: Beavers are part of a {rewilding} project in Scotland.

words.definition: making an exact genetic copy of a plant or animal
words.example: Dolly the sheep was the first mammal created by {cloning} from an adult cell.

words.definition: having had its genes changed by scientists
words.example: Some countries ban {genetically modified} crops.

words.definition: an animal or plant at the very first stage of its growth
words.example: The chick {embryo} develops inside the egg for three weeks.

words.definition: a pill with no medicine in it, used in tests of a new drug
words.example: Half the patients were given a {placebo} instead of the real drug.

words.definition: a test of a new medicine or treatment on volunteers
words.example: The new drug is being tested in a {clinical trial} with 500 volunteers.

words.definition: never having happened before
words.example: No team had ever won four titles in a row; it was an {unprecedented} achievement.

words.definition: the checking of research by other experts before it is published
words.example: Before publication, other scientists checked the study in a process called {peer review}.

words.definition: based on observation and experiment, not on theory
words.example: Their claim rests on {empirical} research: careful observation and experiments, not just theory.

words.definition: to repeat an experiment and get the same result
words.example: To test the discovery, other labs tried to {replicate} the experiment exactly, step by step.

words.definition: the careful watching of people, often in secret
words.example: Cameras are used for {surveillance} in city centres.

words.definition: false information, spread by mistake or on purpose
words.example: The incorrect date was {misinformation}, an honest typing error rather than an attempt to influence anyone.

words.definition: the record of everything you do online
words.example: Every post you share adds to your {digital footprint}.

words.definition: changing an industry or market completely
words.example: Music streaming was a {disruptive} technology: it completely changed how the music industry makes money.

words.definition: a place where people only hear opinions like their own
words.example: Following only people who agree with you creates an {echo chamber}.

words.definition: laws that keep people's personal information safe
words.example: In the UK, {data protection} laws require schools to keep pupils' records secure.

words.definition: seeming to be everywhere
words.example: Smartphones are now {ubiquitous}: you see them everywhere, from buses to classrooms.

words.definition: the state of nobody knowing who you are
words.example: The {anonymity} of the internet lets some people be cruel.

words.definition: making you want to do or have more and more
words.example: These games are {addictive}: once you start playing, it is very hard to stop.

words.definition: one-sided or false information used to influence people
words.example: During the war, the government used posters as {propaganda} to persuade people to support it.

words.definition: reporting news in a shocking way to attract readers
words.example: The paper was accused of {sensationalism} for exaggerating a small story just to sell copies.

words.definition: a newspaper article giving the opinion of the paper itself
words.example: In today's {editorial}, the newspaper gives its own opinion on the new tax.

words.definition: a newspaper with short stories and lots of gossip
words.example: The {tabloid} printed rumours about the footballer's private life.

words.definition: not supporting either side
words.example: Referees must remain {impartial} and never favour either team.

words.definition: careful and detailed examination
words.example: Every line of the minister's spending came under close {scrutiny} from the auditors.

words.definition: to give secret information to the public
words.example: Someone decided to {leak} the report to the press.

words.definition: a person who tells the public about wrongdoing in an organisation
words.example: The {whistle-blower} revealed that the company had hidden the danger.

words.definition: the right of newspapers to report without government control
words.example: Journalists marched to defend {press freedom}.

words.definition: connected with beauty and the way things look
words.example: The concrete building has little {aesthetic} appeal.

words.definition: new and experimental, especially in art
words.example: Her {avant-garde} music was so new and experimental that it seemed decades ahead of its time.

words.definition: a detailed judgement of a piece of work
words.example: The art critic wrote a detailed {critique} of the exhibition, praising some paintings and attacking others.

words.definition: the best piece of work by an artist
words.example: Many people consider this painting his {masterpiece}.

words.definition: using humour to criticise people or ideas
words.example: The show mocks politicians with silly jokes and impressions; it is pure {satire}.

words.definition: a happy but slightly sad feeling about the past
words.example: Old family photos fill me with {nostalgia}.

words.definition: to show someone in a particular way in art or writing
words.example: The film tries to {portray} the queen as kind and wise.

words.definition: bringing strong memories, feelings or images into your mind
words.example: The {evocative} smell of the old house reminded her of childhood summers.

words.definition: belonging to the present time
words.example: Is Shakespeare still relevant to {contemporary} life, or only to the time he lived in?

words.definition: praised by many critics
words.example: The film was widely {acclaimed} by critics and audiences alike.

words.definition: to find new people to join a company or group
words.example: The firm plans to {recruit} fifty graduates and give them jobs this year.

words.definition: having lost your job because it is no longer needed
words.example: Two hundred workers were made {redundant} when the factory closed.

words.definition: something that encourages you to do something
words.example: A bonus is an {incentive} to work harder.

words.definition: a meeting where a manager judges how well an employee is working
words.example: At my annual {performance review}, my manager praised my work and set new goals.

words.definition: to give part of your work to someone else
words.example: Busy managers who try to do everything themselves must learn to {delegate}.

words.definition: working for different companies rather than for one employer
words.example: She works as a {freelance} photographer, taking jobs from many different magazines.

words.definition: meeting people who may be useful for your career
words.example: At conferences, she does a lot of {networking}, meeting people who might help her career.

words.definition: extreme tiredness caused by working too hard for too long
words.example: Working seventy hours a week for months left him exhausted, suffering from {burnout}.

words.definition: a job in which you learn a skill while you work
words.example: He did an {apprenticeship} with a local electrician.

words.definition: a small, visible part of a much bigger problem
words.example: These complaints are only the {tip of the iceberg}.

words.definition: something that seems bad but turns out to be good
words.example: Losing that job seemed terrible, but it was {a blessing in disguise}: I found a better one.

words.definition: to do something cheaply or badly to save time
words.example: Never {cut corners} when checking the brakes.

words.definition: not able to decide between two things
words.example: I'm still {on the fence} about which university to choose.

words.definition: to make people feel relaxed when they first meet
words.example: A silly game helped {break the ice} on the first day.

words.definition: something that has both good and bad effects
words.example: Fame can be {a double-edged sword}: it brings money but also takes away your privacy.

words.text: hit the nail on the head
words.definition: to describe something exactly right
words.example: Your answer was exactly right: you {hit the nail on the head}.

words.definition: the final problem that makes you lose patience
words.example: When the bus broke down too, it was {the last straw}.

words.definition: over a long period of time
words.example: Studying now will pay off {in the long run}.

words.definition: to begin (formal)
words.example: Guests should be seated before noon, when the ceremony will {commence}.

words.definition: to end (formal)
words.example: This train will {terminate} at the next station.

words.definition: to try very hard (formal)
words.example: We will {endeavour} to reply within two working days.

words.definition: to buy (formal)
words.example: Customers may {purchase} tickets at the box office for ten pounds each.

words.definition: enough (formal)
words.example: Two hours will be {sufficient} to finish the test; you won't need more.

words.definition: afterwards (formal)
words.example: He was arrested and {subsequently} released.

words.definition: before (formal)
words.example: Please arrive ten minutes {prior to} your appointment.

words.definition: to ask for information (formal)
words.example: I am writing to {enquire} about your summer courses.

words.definition: the place where someone lives (formal)
words.example: The British prime minister's official {residence} is at 10 Downing Street.

words.definition: to help (formal)
words.example: Staff will {assist} passengers with heavy bags.

words.definition: to get information or a reaction from someone
words.example: The teacher's question failed to {elicit} any reaction from the bored class.

words.definition: not allowed by law or by the rules
words.example: Customs officers found {illicit} goods hidden in the van.

words.definition: careful not to cause embarrassment or attract attention
words.example: Please be {discreet} and keep this news to yourself.

words.definition: separate and different from each other
words.example: The course is split into four {discrete} units, each completely separate from the others.

words.definition: harmful or bad for something
words.example: Heavy frost had an {adverse} effect on the harvest, damaging much of the crop.

words.definition: not liking something or not wanting to do it
words.example: I'm not {averse} to a bit of hard work.

words.definition: to break a rule openly
words.example: Some drivers {flout} the speed limit every day.

words.definition: to show something off so that people notice it
words.example: He likes to {flaunt} his expensive new watch.

words.definition: famous and respected
words.example: She comes from an {eminent} family of judges and professors, respected by everyone.

words.definition: about to happen very soon
words.example: Dark clouds warned that heavy rain was {imminent}.

words.definition: very careful about every small detail
words.example: Her drawings are {meticulous}: every feather on every bird is perfectly detailed.

words.definition: behaving as if you are better than other people
words.example: He's so {arrogant} that he thinks he is better than everyone else in the class.

words.definition: not proud; not thinking you are better than others
words.example: Despite winning the prize, she stayed {humble}, saying her teammates deserved more credit than she did.

words.definition: dealing with problems in a practical way
words.example: She takes a {pragmatic} approach: whatever works is fine with her.

words.definition: working hard and carefully, wanting to do things right
words.example: Out of a sense of duty, the {conscientious} student finished her homework before going out.

words.definition: believing that people only act for themselves
words.example: He's {cynical} about politicians, believing they only make promises to win votes.

words.definition: not giving up easily
words.example: The {tenacious} climber reached the summit on her third attempt.

words.definition: trusting too easily because of lack of experience
words.example: It was {naive} to think the free gift had no catch.

words.definition: having a charm that attracts and inspires people
words.example: Crowds were drawn to the {charismatic} young politician by her magnetic personality, not her arguments.
